title: We still don’t know how people are really using AI
gist: A new academic project called the AI Observatory aggregates consented real-world chatbot conversations to independently assess AI use, finding far more sensitive and personal behavior than the work-focused reports self-published by Anthropic and OpenAI, and arguing that consequential policy decisions are being made on company-controlled data.

insights.claim: AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI publish usage reports but only release the data they want seen, with no independent source to corroborate it, according to Stanford researcher Anka Reuel.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: Reliance on self-reported vendor data means policymakers and investors lack a verifiable picture of real AI usage.
insights.quote: There is no independent source to corroborate it.

insights.claim: The AI Observatory aggregated 85,633 conversational turns across 24,521 conversations from seven consented real-world datasets, spanning 5,000 users and 52 models between 2023 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: Establishes the first cross-model independent baseline, however small, against which company narratives can be checked.

insights.claim: The Observatory's dataset is a drop in the bucket next to the labs' own access, as the latest Anthropic Economic Index analyzed 1 million Claude conversations and OpenAI's report analyzed 1.5 million.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: The scale asymmetry means independent researchers cannot fully substitute for company data, keeping labs' narratives dominant.

insights.claim: Applying Anthropic's own filtering methods to the Observatory dataset would have removed nearly half—48%—of conversations as non-work-related, revealing a large blind spot in the work-focused Anthropic Economic Index.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: Roughly half of real AI use is invisible in the most-cited industry benchmark, distorting policy and market understanding.
insights.locator: When the AI Observatory researchers applied Anthropic’s methods

insights.claim: The filtered-out personal conversations were far more likely to involve harassment and hate (27.5% versus 5.66% in Anthropic's analysis), sexual content (16.7% versus 2.4%), and adult or illicit topics (7.9% versus 2.1%).
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: Sensitive uses are dramatically underrepresented in company reports, understating both risk exposure and content-moderation stakes.

insights.claim: OpenAI's 2025 report similarly found only 30% of consumer ChatGPT use was work-related, corroborating that personal use dominates.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: Confirms across vendors that productivity framings capture a minority of actual usage.

insights.claim: In the WildChat dataset, conversations grew longer and more elaborate over time with more small talk, suggesting rising AI companionship, while AI assistants' self-disclosure that they are chatbots decreased.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: Growing companionship and declining bot self-disclosure signal deepening emotional reliance, a product and safety trend to monitor.

insights.claim: Exchanges labeled sensitive, including sexual harassment and hate speech, became less frequent over time, which might indicate platforms deployed more effective safeguards.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: A tentative sign that safety investments are working, though the consented-data sample likely undercounts sensitive use.

insights.claim: Highly consequential decisions about AI's benefits and risks are currently being made on the basis of very limited, company-controlled data, per Reuel.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: Policy and investment decisions built on vendor-curated data carry systematic blind-spot risk.

insights.claim: Because the Observatory draws only from voluntarily provided data, it probably underrepresents sensitive uses that people are less likely to share, so its findings are not indicative of all AI use.
insights.speaker: Eileen Guo
insights.so_what: The independent dataset's self-selection bias means true sensitive-use rates are likely even higher than measured.
